title: Apparent Volatility Roughness and Perpetual-Futures Funding: Persistent Association, Weak Transition Information
items.abstract: <jats:p>A low Hurst estimate from realized volatility can describe latent variance, measurement error, or both. This paper asks a narrower empirical question: does the apparent roughness of realized volatility align with a directly observed leverage-related state in cryptocurrency perpetual futures? Using public Binance Vision data for BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT from January 2020 through July 2026, I estimate a rolling increment-variance exponent from hourly realized variance and match it to perpetual-futures funding and the perpetual-spot basis. In six-hour update samples, a one-standard-deviation increase in absolute funding is associated with a 0.010 decrease in apparent H for Bitcoin and a 0.006 decrease for Ether. The association survives month fixed effects and alternative 1-, 5-, and 15-minute realized-variance meshes. It does not survive the inclusion of lagged apparent H, and funding does not explain changes in apparent H. Non-overlapping 14-day blocks retain the relation for Bitcoin during extreme funding episodes but not for Ether. Recursive forecasts show no daily gain; an Ether one-hour gain is statistically detectable but economically small and does not generalize. The evidence therefore supports a persistent state association, not a transition signal, structural estimate of spot regularity, or trading rule. The distinction clarifies what a rolling roughness estimate can and cannot identify in noisy high-frequency markets.</jats:p>

title: Conditional and Basket Event-Linked Perpetual Futures: Funding Rates, Pricing and Correlation-Aware Margin
items.abstract: <jats:p>Majumdar (2026a) built a perpetual future and options on a single binary prediction market from three parts: a funding-rate identity that holds the perpetual's mark on the market's probability index, a logit-normal pricer for European options on that index, and a scenario-grid portfolio margin. Nechepurenko (2026b) classified the contracts that can be written on more than one market and proved, for each, a qualitative result; none of them is priced there. We price them. The conditional index $P(A|B)$ is a martingale under the measure conditioned on $B$, and under the pricing measure it drifts. In a bivariate logit model the drift is $-\rho\sigma_c\sigma_b c(1-c)(1-b)$, so the funding rate of a perpetual on it is the single-market identity plus a correction of that size and the opposite sign. On the two nested Polymarket pairs from 2024 that we could calibrate, the correction was a sixth of the base term on one and the larger of the two on half the days on the other. It stays bounded as the conditioning probability falls to zero. What breaks is the mark: an index backed out of two quoted legs carries a half-spread of $(s_q + c\,s_b)/P(B)$, and the one-day 99 percent loss on a unit position rises from 0.083 at $P(B) = 0.5$ to 0.48 at $P(B) = 0.01$. At half a tick per leg the listing floor for a five-cent tolerance is 0.15; at the effective half-spread of about a cent measured on Polymarket's tape it is 0.30. On the one pair whose conditioning leg did fall to zero, Biden's 2024 nomination, the joint market traded above its own conditioning leg on 29 of 189 days, by up to 14 cents, and the leg went from 0.29 to zero in one day. Options on the conditional index are priced by the single-market pricer verbatim when the option is void if $B$ fails, and with one drift term otherwise. For the basket, funding is the weighted sum of the legs' identities. Correlation enters only the margin, and there we compare the one-dimension-per-event grid against the most probable stress found by minimising the rate function of the seven-dimensional logit diffusion, calibrated to the seven 2024 swing-state markets, whose logit innovations have a mean pairwise correlation of 0.38. At a matched 99 percent one-day shock the grid charges 1.48 times the stress margin on a long basket, 1.80 times on a long-short spread and 1.58 times on a covered-call book; with the fixed ten-point shocks of the base case the ratios to the simulated 99 percent loss are 3.7, 4.6 and 6.2. Under equal correlation the gap is $\sqrt{K/(1+(K-1)\rho)}$ for the basket and $\sqrt{2/(1-\rho)}$ for the spread.</jats:p>

title: Limits to Coordination:&nbsp;Funding Drag in Crypto Perpetual Funding Rates
items.abstract: <jats:p>Extreme negative funding rates in cryptocurrency perpetual futures are widely interpreted as reversal signals, but the speed of the subsequent correction varies by an order of magnitude. This paper introduces limits to coordination, a new form of arbitrage constraint operating alongside the capital constraints of Shleifer and Vishny (1997) and the funding-liquidity constraints of Brunnermeier and Pedersen (2009). I document funding drag: the speed of parity restoration after a funding-rate extreme is dominated by realized volatility. Using 1,696 events across 18 Binance perpetual contracts, high-volatility events take a median of 27.0 hours to correct, against 3.0 hours for low-volatility events (log-rank χ 2 = 147.25, p &lt; 0.0001). A one-standard-deviation increase in realized volatility lowers the hazard of correction by approximately 41% (HR = 0.5935; naive SE = 0.0549; contract-clustered SE = 0.0675; year-monthclustered SE = 0.0784). A placebo test on volatility-matched non-event hours shows that only extreme funding-rate events are slow to correct (27.0h vs 10.0h, χ 2 = 88.04, p &lt; 10-20). Four accelerated-failure-time specifications yield time ratios of 2.32-3.72. A recursive-partitioning tree places the strongest heterogeneity at the volatility ratio vol24/vol168, with correction time spanning a 10.6-fold range from 11.53 to 122.62 hours. The effect is present both before and after the FTX collapse (HR 0.570 vs 0.702). The evidence is consistent with a coordinationfailure interpretation, described here as a robust empirical regularity rather than as a structural claim about the mechanism. 1</jats:p>

title: Conditional Arbitrage Capacity: Evidence from Crypto Perpetual Funding Rates
items.abstract: <jats:p>Extreme negative funding rates in cryptocurrency perpetual futures are widely interpreted as reversal signals. This paper shows that the reversal pattern is conditional on market direction. Using 274 funding-rate extreme events across BTC, ETH, and SOL from 2021 to 2026, I find that events on up days revert by +1.88% over the next 24 hours, while events on down days continue by-1.74%. The gap of +3.62 percentage points is statistically significant (block bootstrap 95% CI [2.60, 4.67]) and economically large. Net of funding, the gap is +3.59 percentage points. The pattern is stable around seven exogenous market-wide shocks: within ±30-day windows, the gap is positive in all seven cases (sign test p = 0.00781) and the pooled estimate is +6.47 percentage points (95% CI [4.45, 8.86]). The asymmetry is consistent across 12 year-by-direction cells and 13 coins. Online learning and alternative regime models yield the same conclusion: the asymmetry is structural rather than a signal-quality or regime-specific artifact. I propose conditional arbitrage capacity as a state variable in the limits-to-arbitrage framework: effectiveness depends on capital level and independently on whether the market moves with or against arbitrage capital.</jats:p>
